chunks: "The big differences are pins, speed and who gets selected how.
SPI uses four wires at minimum: clock, MOSI, MISO and a chip-select, and every extra device needs its own chip-select pin.
It's full duplex, since every clock shifts a bit out and a bit in, and the outputs are push-pull, so edges are crisp and you can run at tens of MHz.
I2C uses just two wires, SCL and SDA, shared by everything. Devices are selected by a 7-bit address sent on the bus, so adding a device costs zero pins.
The price is speed: the lines are open-drain with pull-up resistors, so rising edges are slow RC curves and you're limited to 100 kilohertz, 400 kilohertz, or 1 megahertz on a good day.
It's half duplex, and it has more protocol overhead: a start, an address byte, and an ACK bit after every byte.
I2C does give you a few things SPI doesn't: acknowledgement, so you know if a device is actually there, multi-master support with arbitration, and clock stretching.
So I'd pick I2C for lots of slow devices like sensors and EEPROMs, and SPI for anything that needs bandwidth, like flash, displays or fast ADCs."
